header.title: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP)
header.description: Build a linear model where some variables can be continuous, integer, or binary/Boolean. The feasible set is no longer only a convex polyhedron: integrality restricts admissible points to a discrete lattice, so the solver searches a branch-and-bound tree over LP relaxations.

import.info_body: A MILP JSON file extends the LP schema with variables[].integrality. Use C for continuous, I for integer, and B for binary/Boolean variables. Binary variables are normalized to bounds [0, 1]. Optional solver settings can include time_limit and mip_gap.

vars.hint: Choose the mathematical domain of each decision variable: continuous, integer, or binary.

solver.hint: MILP solve time can grow quickly. Use an optional time limit or relative MIP gap when a good incumbent is enough.
solver.info_body: Time limit stops the search after the given number of seconds. If the solver has an incumbent, status can be Feasible: the solution satisfies all constraints but is not proven optimal. MIP gap is the relative distance between the incumbent and the best bound; smaller values require stronger proof and can take longer.

header.title: Knapsack
header.description: Choose the knapsack variant, then describe items, capacities, and decision limits. The current executable variant is 0/1 Knapsack; the switch prepares the UI for the next variants.

variant.hint: Select the mathematical meaning of each decision variable. The 0/1 variant is fully implemented; the other modes define the next formulation panels.

descriptions.zero_one: Each item can be selected once or excluded: x_i is binary.
descriptions.bounded: Each item can be selected an integer quantity up to a maximum limit: 0 <= x_i <= u_i.
descriptions.unbounded: Each item can be selected any non-negative integer quantity, limited only by capacity.
descriptions.fractional: A fraction of each item can be selected: x_i is continuous between 0 and 1.
descriptions.multi_dimensional: Each selected item consumes several resources at once, such as weight, volume, time, or budget.

placeholders.bounded: Next step: add a quantity-limit column per item and solve x_i as an integer quantity between 0 and its maximum.
placeholders.unbounded: Next step: reuse item value/weight rows but solve quantities x_i in the non-negative integers without per-item upper bounds.
placeholders.fractional: Next step: keep value and weight rows, then solve fractions greedily by value/weight ratio and display selected percentages.
placeholders.multi_dimensional: Next step: add a resource table with one capacity per dimension and item consumption columns for each resource.

capacity.label: Maximum capacity
capacity.info_body: Capacity is the maximum total weight that the selected items may use.
capacity.info_html:
Rule

The solver enforces sum weight_i x_i <= capacity.

Input

Capacity must be a non-negative integer because the current exact dynamic-programming algorithm indexes capacities from 0 to C.

Scale

The running time grows with number_of_items * capacity. Large capacities may require a MILP or another knapsack algorithm.

items.hint: Enter one row per item. Value can be decimal; weight and capacity must be non-negative integers.
items.info_body: Each row describes one item that can be selected at most once.
items.info_html:
Decision variable

For every item Optees creates a binary variable x_i: 1 means selected, 0 means excluded.

Value

The value is the contribution to the objective. Optees maximizes total selected value.

Weight

The weight consumes capacity and must be an integer in the current DP solver.

formula.body: max Σ valueᵢ xᵢ subject to Σ weightᵢ xᵢ ≤ capacity and xᵢ ∈ {0, 1}. The dynamic-programming solver is exact for this 0/1 model, but pseudo-polynomial in capacity.
formula.info_body: Optees solves the first Knapsack implementation with an exact dynamic-programming algorithm.
formula.info_html:
State

dp[i][w] stores the best value reachable with the first i items and capacity w.

Transition

For each item, the algorithm compares excluding it with including it if it fits.

Guarantee

For integer weights and capacity, this gives a proven optimal 0/1 solution.

header.title: Linear Programming (LP)
header.description: Linear programming helps you maximize or minimize a value (like profit or cost) subject to a set of conditions. Solutions are decimal numbers, perfect for problems where resources can be divided.

import.schema_intro: The file must be a JSON object with the following structure. Use null for unbounded variables (−∞ / +∞).

example.title: LP examples
example.intro: Use these examples as small templates when you model a continuous linear optimization problem.

block1.title: Production mix
block1.body: A workshop produces chairs and tables. Let X1 be chairs and X2 be tables. If each chair earns 30 and each table earns 50, maximize z = 30 X1 + 50 X2. Capacity constraints can be 2 X1 + 4 X2 <= 80 for machine hours and X1 + X2 <= 30 for storage. Bounds X1, X2 >= 0 mean fractional production is allowed.

block2.title: Diet or blending
block2.body: A nutrition example minimizes cost while satisfying minimum nutrients. Let X1 and X2 be kilograms of two ingredients. Minimize z = 4 X1 + 7 X2 with constraints such as 3 X1 + X2 >= 12 proteins and X1 + 2 X2 >= 10 vitamins. Use >= constraints when a requirement must be at least a threshold.

block3.title: Multiple optimal solutions
block3.body: For max z = X1 + X2 with X1 + X2 <= 6 and X1, X2 >= 0, every point on the segment X1 + X2 = 6 is optimal. The solver reports z* = 6 and ranges X1 in [0, 6], X2 in [0, 6].

block4.title: 3D test case
block4.body: Try this small 3-variable model: max z = X1 + X2 + X3, subject to X1 + X2 + X3 <= 6 and X1, X2, X3 >= 0. The optimal face is a triangle: z* = 6, each variable ranges in [0, 6], and there are infinitely many optimal solutions.

problem.title: LP problem description
problem.intro: Linear programming solves optimization problems whose objective and constraints are linear functions of continuous decision variables.

block1.title: Mathematical form
block1.body: A canonical LP can be written as min or max c^T x + offset subject to A_ub x <= b_ub, A_eq x = b_eq, and lower/upper bounds on x. The vector x contains the decision variables; c contains objective coefficients; A and b encode the constraints.

block2.title: Feasible region and optimum
block2.body: The constraints define a convex polyhedron. A linear objective reaches its optimum at a face of that polyhedron: often a single vertex, sometimes an edge, a plane, or a higher-dimensional face. When the optimal face has positive dimension, the model has infinitely many optimal solutions.

block3.title: Algorithmic behavior
block3.body: Optees calls SciPy/HiGHS through linprog. Maximization models are converted to minimization by changing the sign of c. After solving, statuses are mapped to Optimal, Infeasible, Unbounded, or NotSolved, and HiGHS diagnostics are preserved for the UI.

block4.title: Optimal ranges
block4.body: After an optimum z* is found, Optees adds the equality c^T x = z* and solves auxiliary LPs min x_i and max x_i for each variable. This gives the exact interval of optimal values for each variable. Pseudocode: solve original LP; add c^T x = z*; for every i solve min x_i and max x_i.

bounds.hint: Empty = ±∞. You can type fractions (e.g., 1/2) or 'inf'.
